parsed_record.title: A SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR INLINE DUAL-WAVELENGTH OPTICAL DETECTION OF MICROPLASTICS IN FLOWING WATER
parsed_record.abstract: The invention relates to optical sensing and water-quality monitoring, and discloses an inline system for continuous detection of microplastics in flowing water. Water passes through a flow-through optical chamber (2) from a water inlet unit (1), where dual-wavelength LED light sources (3) at about 450 nm and 620 nm, a primary polarizer (4), and a secondary cross polarizer (6) arranged at about 90 degrees enhance scattered-light discrimination at a microplastic detection zone (5). A high-sensitivity photodiode receiver (7) converts the scattered optical response into an electrical signal, which is conditioned by a signal conditioning circuit (8) and processed by an ESP32 microcontroller unit (9) to determine presence and approximate concentration of microplastics. Processed data are transmitted through a Wi-Fi communication module (10) to a cloud database (11), displayed on a web monitoring dashboard (12), and used to trigger a mobile alert system (13). The system provides low-cost, portable, real-time monitoring. Fig. 1 best characterises the invention.
parsed_record.specification:
Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION
The present invention generally relates to environmental water-quality monitoring and optical sensing systems, and more particularly to an inline dual-wavelength optical sensor system and method for real-time detection and monitoring of microplastics in flowing water.
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
The subject matter lies in the field of optical sensing systems for environmental water-quality monitoring, and more particularly in the detection of microplastic contamination in flowing water bodies and water-handling systems. Microplastics have emerged as a significant concern in rivers, lakes, reservoirs, irrigation canals, wastewater streams, drinking-water sources, and aquaculture environments because of their persistence, mobility, and potential entry into ecological and human-use pathways. In practice, however, reliable identification of microplastic particles in water remains technically difficult. Water from natural and managed sources commonly contains sediments, algae, organic debris, colloidal matter, and other suspended impurities that produce overlapping optical or physical responses, with the result that conventional water-quality measurements are often unable to distinguish plastic particles with sufficient specificity. There is therefore a recognised need in this technical field for monitoring approaches that are suitable for direct deployment in flowing water and capable of producing timely information during contamination events.
Existing techniques used for microplastic analysis are predominantly laboratory-centred. Analytical methods such as Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, microscopy-based examination, and related confirmatory techniques are useful for material identification, but they generally depend upon manual sample collection, sample transport, preparation under controlled conditions, and operation by trained personnel. Such methods are comparatively expensive and time-consuming, and they are not well suited for continuous observation at distributed field locations. In many practical monitoring situations, especially in irrigation systems, open channels, reservoirs, industrial discharge points, and remote environmental sites, the delay between sampling and analysis can reduce the value of the information for operational response or pollution management.
Various optical particle-sensing arrangements have also been employed to detect suspended matter in fluids by measuring scattering, attenuation, turbidity, or related optical effects. These systems may estimate particle load or indicate variations in water quality, but they commonly function as general particle monitors rather than selective detectors of microplastics. Their performance may degrade in the presence of mixed contaminants because natural suspended solids and biological material can generate signals similar to those of plastic particles. In addition, many known optical systems are developed for benchtop or controlled-use settings, rely upon precise optical alignment or specialised instrumentation, or are not configured for long-duration unattended use in outdoor flow conditions. Remote communication, historical data retention, and immediate alerting functions are also not consistently available in conventional arrangements.
US10274369B2, directed to an optical particle monitoring system, discloses the use of light scattering measurements for analysis of particle concentration and estimation of particle density. This document is relevant in that it recognises optical scattering as a basis for assessing particulate content in a fluid. However, the disclosed approach is directed to particle monitoring at a general level and does not provide selective discrimination of microplastic particles from other suspended contaminants typically present in environmental water. The document also does not address embedded intelligent processing for field interpretation or networked remote environmental surveillance.
US10908133B2 discloses a fluid analysis device for detecting suspended particles through optical measurement techniques. The reference is relevant because it concerns optical characterisation of particles in a fluid medium. Nevertheless, the disclosure is associated with controlled analytical conditions and a comparatively complex optical arrangement, making it less suited to portable inline deployment in natural or utility water flows such as rivers, irrigation canals, or wastewater streams. The need for specialised analytical equipment and controlled operation limits its practical utility for routine real-time field monitoring of microplastic contamination.
US11105879B2, entitled optical detection system for water quality analysis, focuses on optical sensing of turbidity and suspended solids. This prior art is relevant to general water-quality monitoring and demonstrates the use of optical sensors in aqueous environments. Even so, turbidity-oriented systems primarily indicate the presence of suspended matter in aggregate and are not able to accurately differentiate microplastics from mineral sediments, biological impurities, or organic particulates. The disclosure is therefore informative for overall water-condition assessment, but it does not adequately address the selectivity problem that arises in mixed environmental samples.
US20180356211A1, entitled systems and methods for particle detection using optical sensors, describes a particle detection arrangement employing laser illumination and photodetectors for estimating suspended particles in fluid samples. This reference shows that optical interrogation of particles in a liquid medium is known. However, the described system is principally oriented to laboratory-style particle analysis and does not disclose a configuration specifically adapted for dedicated microplastic identification in flowing environmental water. It also does not address the practical difficulties associated with field deployment, variable background contaminants, and continuous monitoring over distributed water infrastructure.
WO2021219876A1 discloses a water-quality monitoring platform in which multiple environmental sensors are interconnected through IoT networks for remote observation of parameters such as pH, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, and temperature. This document is relevant because it illustrates the growing importance of networked and remotely accessible water monitoring architectures. At the same time, the platform is directed to conventional water-quality parameters and does not include dedicated optical sensing mechanisms for detecting microplastics or distinguishing such particles on the basis of wavelength-dependent optical behaviour. As a result, while useful for broad environmental monitoring, it does not resolve the problem of specific microplastic surveillance in flowing water.
The known approaches and cited documents collectively show that the art has addressed either detailed laboratory identification of particles, general optical measurement of suspended matter, or remote monitoring of standard water-quality parameters. A persistent difficulty remains in reconciling these areas within practical field conditions. Laboratory methods offer material analysis but are costly, delayed, and operationally intensive. General optical sensors may provide continuous readings but often lack selectivity in waters containing sediments, algae, and organic load. IoT-based environmental platforms improve accessibility of data but do not, by themselves, provide a sensing basis for recognising microplastics. Further, many existing systems are not readily scalable across multiple monitoring points because of equipment cost, maintenance burden, operator dependence, and the need for controlled measurement conditions.
Accordingly, there remains a requirement in the art for an approach to monitoring microplastic contamination in flowing water that is more suitable for routine field deployment, continuous observation, timely reporting, and practical use across environmental, agricultural, industrial, and water-management settings. In view of the deficiencies of existing techniques and the cited prior art, there is a continuing need for improvements relevant to A System and Method for Inline Dual-Wavelength Optical Detection of Microplastics in Flowing Water.
OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION
An object of the invention is to provide an inline microplastic monitoring system for flowing water, wherein a flow-through optical chamber permits continuous sensing of water passing through a defined detection region without interrupting normal flow, thereby avoiding repeated manual sampling and delayed laboratory analysis.
Another object of the invention is to provide a compact optical detection arrangement employing dual-wavelength illumination, preferably at about 450 nm and about 620 nm, so as to obtain differentiated optical responses from suspended particles and thereby improve the identification of microplastic particles in comparison with conventional single-wavelength or general turbidity-based systems.
Another object of the invention is to provide a crossed-polarization based sensing configuration in which a primary polarizer polarizes incident light and a secondary polarizer disposed substantially at 90 degrees suppresses directly transmitted light, whereby scattered light originating from microplastic particles is enhanced for improved selectivity and reduced optical interference from non-target constituents.
Yet another object of the invention is to provide a photodiode-based detection system capable of receiving scattered optical signals and converting the same into corresponding electrical signals, thereby enabling a sensitive, low-cost, and field-deployable alternative to bulky and expensive laboratory instrumentation.
Another object of the invention is to provide signal conditioning and embedded processing means for amplifying, filtering, stabilizing, digitizing, and analyzing the photodiode output through a microcontroller, preferably an ESP32 microcontroller, such that the presence and approximate concentration of microplastics can be determined in real time by threshold-based or programmed analytical routines.
Another object of the invention is to provide an integrated monitoring platform in which selective optical sensing, crossed-polarization analysis, photodiode detection, and embedded real-time processing are combined within a single compact inline device specifically configured for continuous microplastic detection in flowing water, which integrated combination distinguishes the invention from prior systems relying on isolated sensing or offline analysis.
Another object of the invention is to provide an IoT-enabled communication arrangement for wirelessly transmitting processed sensor data to a cloud database, thereby allowing remote access, real-time visualization, centralized monitoring, and storage of historical measurements for trend analysis and environmental surveillance.
Another object of the invention is to provide an automatic alert mechanism configured to compare detected microplastic concentration with one or more predefined threshold values and to generate warning notifications, including SMS, email, or mobile application alerts, when contamination exceeds permissible or selected levels, thereby enabling timely intervention.
Yet another object of the invention is to provide a portable, low-cost, and low-power microplastic monitoring system using affordable optical components, embedded electronics, and rechargeable power support, with optional solar-power compatibility, so that the system may be practically deployed in remote or distributed field locations.
Another object of the invention is to provide a scalable and field-deployable monitoring solution suitable for rivers, lakes, reservoirs, irrigation canals, wastewater channels, and industrial discharge points, wherein multiple sensing units may be networked to a centralized platform for sustained environmental monitoring, reduced dependence on skilled personnel, and improved water-resource management.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The present invention provides a field-deployable, continuous, and real-time system for detecting microplastic contamination in flowing water. The system integrates a Water Inlet Unit (1), Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2), Dual-Wavelength LED Light Sources (3), Primary Polarizer (4), Microplastic Detection Zone (5), Secondary Cross Polarizer (6), High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7), Signal Conditioning Circuit (8), ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9), Wi-Fi Communication Module (10), Cloud Database (11), Web Monitoring Dashboard (12), Mobile Alert System (13), together with power supply, battery backup, voltage regulation, local display, status indication, control, protective enclosure, and data storage components. These components operate together as a compact and integrated monitoring platform.
Water continuously enters through the Water Inlet Unit (1) and passes through the Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2), providing a controlled sensing region under actual flowing-water conditions. Dual-wavelength LED sources operating at approximately 450 nm and 620 nm illuminate the detection zone through the Primary Polarizer (4). Microplastic particles interact with the polarized light and produce characteristic scattered optical responses based on their size, shape, surface characteristics, and material properties.
The Secondary Cross Polarizer (6), positioned approximately 90° relative to the Primary Polarizer (4), suppresses directly transmitted and specularly reflected light while allowing relevant scattered light to reach the High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7). The photodiode converts the optical response into an electrical signal, which is amplified, filtered, stabilized, and processed by the Signal Conditioning Circuit (8) and ESP32 Microcontroller (9) to determine the presence and approximate concentration of microplastics.
The processed measurements are displayed locally, stored in the Data Storage Memory Module (21), and transmitted through the Wi-Fi Communication Module (10) to the Cloud Database (11). The Web Monitoring Dashboard (12) enables remote viewing of real-time and historical measurements. When the detected microplastic concentration exceeds a predefined threshold, the Mobile Alert System (13) generates an automatic notification through SMS, email, mobile application messaging, or dashboard indication.
The system is further supported by a rechargeable battery backup, voltage regulation circuit, LCD display, status indicators, control buttons, and waterproof protective enclosure, enabling reliable and practical field deployment.
Overall, the invention combines inline flow analysis, dual-wavelength optical sensing, crossed-polarization detection, embedded processing, IoT-based communication, cloud data management, and automated early-warning alerts into a single system. It provides a continuous, real-time, compact, scalable, and economically deployable solution for monitoring microplastic contamination in rivers, lakes, reservoirs, irrigation canals, industrial outlets, and other water pathways.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION
The present invention is subsequently described herein using various embodiments. Throughout this description, the term 'may' is used in a permissive sense, indicating the potential to, rather than in a mandatory sense, indicating a requirement. Additionally, the words 'a' or 'an' signify at least one, and the word 'plurality' signifies 'one or more' unless otherwise specified. Moreover, the terminology and phraseology employed herein are solely for descriptive purposes and should not be construed as limiting in scope. Terms such as 'including', 'comprising', 'having', 'containing', or 'involving', and their variations, are intended to be broad and encompass the listed subject matter thereafter, as well as equivalents and additional subject matter not explicitly mentioned, and should not be interpreted as excluding other additives, components, integers, or steps. Similarly, the term 'comprising' is considered synonymous with the terms 'including' or 'containing' for applicable legal purposes.
The present invention relates to a system and method for continuous monitoring of microplastic contamination in flowing water by using optical scattering and polarization behaviour of suspended particles. The invention provides an inline sensing arrangement in which water is allowed to pass continuously through a controlled optical region, irradiated with dual-wavelength light, and examined through crossed polarization so that scattered light attributable to microplastic particles may be detected and converted into an electrical signal for further processing. The invention is particularly directed to field-deployable monitoring where rapid detection, remote access to measurements, and automatic warning capability are required without repeated manual sample collection and without immediate dependence on laboratory analysis.
The invention is based on the integrated use of a flow-through optical chamber, dual-wavelength illumination at approximately 450 nm and approximately 620 nm, a primary polarizer, a secondary cross polarizer positioned at approximately 90 degrees relative to the primary polarizer, a high-sensitivity photodiode receiver, signal conditioning electronics, an ESP32 microcontroller unit, wireless communication, cloud-based storage, dashboard visualization, and an automatic alert mechanism. The novelty lies in the compact and coordinated integration of selective optical detection, embedded real-time analysis, continuous inline operation, Internet-enabled communication, and automated threshold-based warning within a single monitoring platform specifically adapted for microplastic detection in flowing water. The terms a or an, as used herein, may mean at least one, and the term plurality may mean one or more, unless the context requires otherwise. The terms comprising, including, having, involving, and variations thereof are intended to be inclusive in nature, such that the recited features may include additional features, elements, or steps. Any expression such as comprises, but not limited to is intended to indicate that the listed elements are exemplary and non-exhaustive.
A Water Inlet Unit (1) may be provided as an entry interface through which water from a river, lake, reservoir, irrigation canal, wastewater line, industrial discharge stream, or another flowing source is directed toward the sensing section. The Water Inlet Unit (1) may be connected downstream to a Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2). The Water Inlet Unit (1) may be shaped or arranged to admit water in a substantially steady manner so that the sensing region receives a representative flow stream. The Water Inlet Unit (1) may be formed from materials suitable for water contact and field use, and may be assembled as part of a portable or fixed installation. The functional role of the Water Inlet Unit (1) is to introduce the monitored fluid into the optical path while supporting continuous operation rather than batch sampling.
The Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2) may receive water from the Water Inlet Unit (1) and may define a controlled transparent sensing path through which the flowing water passes during measurement. The chamber may be arranged with a geometry that supports stable optical interrogation and may be configured to reduce turbulence and air bubble presence, because such disturbances may otherwise alter scattering behaviour and reduce measurement reliability. The chamber may be transparent in at least the optical path region so that light from the illumination assembly may enter, interact with suspended particles in the water, and be observed by the detection assembly. The chamber may be elongated, tubular, channel-like, or otherwise shaped to support inline flow, provided that the disclosed function of maintaining a sensing region in the water path is achieved. The chamber therefore acts as the physical interface between hydraulic movement and optical analysis.
Dual-Wavelength LED Light Sources (3) may be positioned relative to the Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2) so as to direct light into the water passing through the sensing region. The disclosed light sources provide illumination at approximately 450 nm and approximately 620 nm. These two wavelengths may be used because suspended microplastic particles may exhibit differing optical responses when illuminated at different wavelengths, and the availability of more than one wavelength may improve discrimination relative to sediments, organic matter, or other impurities. The light sources may be mounted in an aligned or angular orientation with respect to the chamber according to the intended optical path. The light sources may be compact solid-state emitters selected for low power consumption and suitability for portable instrumentation. The use of dual-wavelength illumination contributes to selectivity of the system because the detected optical response may be interpreted in light of wavelength-dependent scattering behaviour rather than solely on single-intensity observation.
A Primary Polarizer (4) may be disposed in the illumination path between the Dual-Wavelength LED Light Sources (3) and the Microplastic Detection Zone (5). The Primary Polarizer (4) may convert emitted light into polarized illumination before the light enters the water under analysis. This polarization step may improve the ability of the system to differentiate directly transmitted light from light scattered by suspended particles. The Primary Polarizer (4) may be arranged in a fixed orientation relative to the illumination axis. The material of the polarizer may be any suitable polarizing optical material capable of transmitting the intended wavelengths while imposing polarization on the incident light. By preparing the light in a known polarization state, the Primary Polarizer (4) establishes the optical condition necessary for subsequent crossed-polarization analysis.
The Microplastic Detection Zone (5) may be defined within the interior region of the Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2) where the polarized dual-wavelength light interacts with the flowing water. The Microplastic Detection Zone (5) is not merely an empty volume, but a measurement region in which suspended particles are optically interrogated while the water remains in motion. When microplastic particles pass through this zone, they may scatter the polarized incident light. The nature and magnitude of the scattered optical response may depend on physical characteristics of the particles, including their presence within the optical field and their interaction with the selected wavelengths and polarization condition. The location and extent of the Microplastic Detection Zone (5) may be established by the overlap of the illumination beam, the chamber path, and the receiver field of view.
A Secondary Cross Polarizer (6) may be positioned optically after the Microplastic Detection Zone (5) and before a High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7). The Secondary Cross Polarizer (6) may be oriented approximately 90 degrees relative to the Primary Polarizer (4). By arranging the polarizers in a crossed relationship, the system may suppress directly transmitted or non-scattered light and may thereby enhance sensitivity to light that has changed due to scattering by suspended particles. The Secondary Cross Polarizer (6) thus performs a selective rejection function, reducing background optical contribution and improving optical contrast associated with microplastic-related scattering. The approximately 90 degree orientation is significant because it establishes the crossed polarization condition required for attenuation of the direct optical path. The Secondary Cross Polarizer (6) may be held in a stable optical mount relative to the photodiode receiver and chamber.
The High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7) may be located to receive the scattered optical signal that passes through the Secondary Cross Polarizer (6). The photodiode may convert incident optical energy into an electrical signal whose magnitude is proportional to the detected scattered light. Since the photodiode output may be small and susceptible to noise, the photodiode is disclosed as a high-sensitivity receiver suitable for low-level optical measurements. The High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7) may be electrically coupled to a Signal Conditioning Circuit (8). The receiver may be positioned so that it is responsive to the desired scattered light component from the Microplastic Detection Zone (5), while minimizing undesired direct exposure. The photodiode therefore forms the principal transduction element that converts an optical phenomenon into a measurable electrical parameter for embedded analysis.
The Signal Conditioning Circuit (8) may receive the electrical output from the High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7) and may amplify, filter, and stabilize the received signal prior to digital processing. Amplification may increase the signal magnitude to a level suitable for reliable acquisition. Filtering may suppress noise and unwanted fluctuation that may arise from ambient interference, component noise, or hydraulic disturbance. Stabilization may improve consistency of the signal delivered to the digital controller. The Signal Conditioning Circuit (8) may be implemented using analog electronic stages mounted on an electronic board and electrically connected between the photodiode receiver and an ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9). The role of the Signal Conditioning Circuit (8) is therefore to transform a raw photodiode output into a conditioned signal that may be interpreted with greater reliability by the digital processing section.
The ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9) may be connected to the Signal Conditioning Circuit (8) for acquisition of the conditioned sensor signal. The microcontroller may digitize and process the incoming signal and may execute programmed threshold-based analysis to determine the presence and approximate concentration of microplastics in the flowing water. The microcontroller may compare measured optical responses against predefined thresholds and may produce output values representing contamination level, status condition, or warning state. The ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9) may also coordinate system timing, component operation, local display functions, memory functions, and communication functions. By integrating signal interpretation into the sensing platform itself, the invention avoids dependence on off-site laboratory evaluation for immediate detection decisions.
A Wi-Fi Communication Module (10) may be operatively associated with the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9) to transmit processed data wirelessly from the sensing unit to remote digital infrastructure. In one arrangement, the communication function may be integrated with the microcontroller platform. The Wi-Fi Communication Module (10) may communicate with a Cloud Database (11), thereby allowing sensor readings to be uploaded in real time or near real time. The transmitted information may include measurement values, timestamps, sensor identification, location information, and concentration-related outputs generated by the processing algorithm. The use of wireless communication contributes directly to remote observability, distributed deployment, and centralized environmental surveillance.
The Cloud Database (11) may receive and store data transmitted through the Wi-Fi Communication Module (10). The stored data may include real-time and historical measurements so that contamination events and temporal trends may be reviewed subsequently. A Web Monitoring Dashboard (12) may access the Cloud Database (11) and present the stored and incoming information in a viewable form for an operator or monitoring authority. The dashboard may display current contamination level, historical trends, sensor status, location-linked data, and warning indications. These components collectively extend the sensing system beyond local measurement and permit geographically separated supervision of multiple installed units.
A Mobile Alert System (13) may be linked to the processed data pathway so that an alert is generated when a measured or estimated microplastic concentration exceeds a predefined threshold. The alert may be delivered through SMS, email, or a mobile application, as disclosed. The Mobile Alert System (13) may obtain the threshold event from the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9), from the Cloud Database (11), or through the dashboard-linked infrastructure, depending on implementation. The technical function of the Mobile Alert System (13) is to convert a threshold exceedance into a timely actionable notification, thereby supporting intervention without waiting for periodic manual review of stored data.
A Power Supply Module (14) may provide operational electrical power to the sensing, processing, display, communication, and alert-related electronics. A Rechargeable Battery Backup Unit (15) may be connected with the Power Supply Module (14) so that the system may remain functional during interruption or absence of primary power. Such battery support is particularly suitable for field deployment where grid continuity may be uncertain. A Voltage Regulation Circuit (16) may be connected between the power source and the electrical modules to provide regulated voltage suitable for the optical sources, signal conditioning electronics, control electronics, communication circuitry, and user interface elements. Stable voltage delivery is of practical importance because fluctuation in supply may otherwise affect optical output intensity, analog signal quality, digital processing stability, and communication performance.
An LCD Display Module (17) may be connected to the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9) to provide local display of system information. The displayed information may include operational status, measured contamination level, warning conditions, or other monitoring information available within the device. Status Indicator LEDs (18) may be provided as local visual indicators for operating, standby, communication, or warning states. System Control Buttons (19) may permit local interaction, such as initiating operation, selecting a function, resetting a condition, or navigating local display options. These elements support on-site handling of the unit and may be useful where the system is deployed in a distributed field network but still requires occasional local inspection or service.
A Waterproof Protective Enclosure (20) may house the optical, electrical, and control components of the system in a protected arrangement suitable for environmental deployment. The enclosure may isolate the internal electronics from ambient water exposure, splashing, dust, and external handling conditions encountered in field use. The enclosure may support portable use or fixed mounting adjacent to the monitored water path. A Data Storage Memory Module (21) may also be associated with the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9) to provide local storage of monitoring information. The Data Storage Memory Module (21) may retain measurements where wireless communication is temporarily unavailable or may maintain a local record in addition to cloud storage. The enclosure and memory arrangement contribute to robustness and continuity of operation in practical deployment conditions.
In operation, water entering through the Water Inlet Unit (1) may flow continuously through the Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2) and into the Microplastic Detection Zone (5). The Dual-Wavelength LED Light Sources (3) may direct approximately 450 nm light and approximately 620 nm light toward the flowing water, and the light may first pass through the Primary Polarizer (4) so that polarized illumination is established. Within the Microplastic Detection Zone (5), suspended particles present in the water may interact with the polarized illumination. Microplastic particles may produce scattered light responses that differ from directly transmitted light and may also exhibit distinguishable optical behaviour under the selected wavelengths. The Secondary Cross Polarizer (6), oriented approximately 90 degrees relative to the Primary Polarizer (4), may suppress directly transmitted light and permit enhanced observation of relevant scattered light. The High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7) may then receive the scattered optical signal and convert that signal into an electrical output.
The electrical output from the High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7) may be delivered to the Signal Conditioning Circuit (8), where the signal is amplified, filtered, and stabilized before being supplied to the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9). The microcontroller may acquire the conditioned signal, perform threshold-based analysis, determine the presence of microplastics, and estimate approximate concentration. The processed data may then be transmitted through the Wi-Fi Communication Module (10) to the Cloud Database (11), where timestamped and location-associated records may be stored. The Web Monitoring Dashboard (12) may present real-time and historical measurements to a remote user. When the estimated concentration exceeds a predefined threshold, the Mobile Alert System (13) may generate an alert through SMS, email, or a mobile application. During operation, the Power Supply Module (14), Rechargeable Battery Backup Unit (15), and Voltage Regulation Circuit (16) maintain electrical continuity, while the LCD Display Module (17), Status Indicator LEDs (18), System Control Buttons (19), Waterproof Protective Enclosure (20), and Data Storage Memory Module (21) support local usability and reliability.
A disclosed implementation of the invention comprises installation of the Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2) in a water pathway so that water from a river, lake, reservoir, irrigation canal, or other source continuously passes through the sensing region. In this implementation, the Dual-Wavelength LED Light Sources (3) are positioned to illuminate the flowing water, the Primary Polarizer (4) and Secondary Cross Polarizer (6) are arranged to reduce unwanted reflections and improve optical contrast of scattered light, the High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7) detects the resulting optical signal, and the Signal Conditioning Circuit (8) prepares the electrical output for analysis by the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9). This implementation demonstrates the best disclosed manner of carrying out the invention because it includes the full sequence of inline sensing, optical discrimination, electrical conversion, signal conditioning, embedded analysis, communication, storage, visualization, and alert generation in one coordinated arrangement.
Another disclosed implementation comprises the repeated sensing cycle in which the system continuously performs illumination, scattering detection, signal conditioning, concentration estimation, wireless transmission, cloud storage, dashboard display, and automatic threshold monitoring. This implementation demonstrates that the invention is not limited to a single measurement event, but is adapted for sustained monitoring over time. The stored data may support trend analysis, while the remote dashboard and alert system may support environmental or agricultural water-quality management. The use cases expressly disclosed for deployment include rivers, lakes, reservoirs, irrigation canals, wastewater systems, industrial discharge points, and other water-monitoring locations. These use cases show that the invention may be scaled through deployment of multiple sensing units connected to a centralized monitoring platform, without altering the fundamental interaction among the disclosed optical, electronic, and communication components.
An embodiment of the present invention may use the same component arrangement in a portable installation powered through the Power Supply Module (14) and supported by the Rechargeable Battery Backup Unit (15), thereby enabling operation where continuous primary power is unavailable. An embodiment of the present invention may support low-power field use and may be adapted for potential solar-power support where such support is provided externally to the disclosed power arrangement. An embodiment of the present invention may use local storage in the Data Storage Memory Module (21) as a temporary or supplemental record when cloud connectivity is intermittent. An embodiment of the present invention may present local operating information through the LCD Display Module (17) and Status Indicator LEDs (18) while also maintaining remote access through the Web Monitoring Dashboard (12). An embodiment of the present invention may be installed as a single stand-alone monitoring unit or as part of a distributed network of plural sensing units communicating with a centralized cloud-based monitoring platform.
An embodiment of the present invention may retain the disclosed dual-wavelength and crossed-polarizer optical principle while varying the physical arrangement of the optical components within the Waterproof Protective Enclosure (20) or relative to the Flow-Through Optical Chamber (2), provided that polarized illumination interacts with flowing water in the Microplastic Detection Zone (5) and scattered light is selectively received by the High-Sensitivity Photodiode Receiver (7). An embodiment of the present invention may use any suitable transparent chamber form, optical mounting configuration, or field enclosure configuration compatible with the disclosed operation. An embodiment of the present invention may employ the same threshold-based determination through the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9) with predefined thresholds selected according to the intended monitoring application. Such variations do not depart from the disclosed inventive concept because the technical contribution resides in the integrated inline combination of selective optical sensing, real-time embedded processing, wireless communication, cloud-linked monitoring, and automatic warning for microplastic detection in flowing water.
The invention provides real-time detection of microplastic particles in flowing water without waiting for laboratory analysis, continuous inline monitoring without repeated manual sampling, and improved detection accuracy through dual-wavelength sensing with crossed-polarization analysis. The invention may reduce interference from suspended sediments, organic matter, and other impurities by suppressing directly transmitted light and emphasizing scattered optical response. The use of optical components, a photodiode receiver, and embedded electronics supports a low-cost and compact design, while the ESP32 Microcontroller Unit (9) enables automated signal processing and concentration estimation. Wireless communication to the Cloud Database (11), visualization through the Web Monitoring Dashboard (12), and warning through the Mobile Alert System (13) provide remote monitoring, historical data storage, trend analysis, and early intervention capability. The portable, field-deployable, low-power, and scalable nature of the disclosed arrangement supports environmental protection, water-resource management, agricultural water-quality monitoring, and reduced dependence on skilled personnel and sophisticated laboratory infrastructure.
Various modifications to these embodiments are evident to those skilled in the art based on the description. The principles associated with the various embodiments described herein can be applied to additional embodiments. Consequently, the description is not intended to be limited to the embodiments but aims to provide the broadest scope consistent with the principles and the innovative and inventive features disclosed or suggested herein. Therefore, the invention is expected to encompass all other such alternatives, modifications, and variations falling within the scope of the present invention.
parsed_record.claims:
1.	A system for real-time detection of microplastics in flowing water, comprising a flow-through optical chamber, dual-wavelength light sources, a primary polarizer, a secondary cross polarizer, a photodiode receiver, a signal-conditioning circuit, and an embedded microcontroller configured to detect and estimate microplastic concentration.
2.	The system of claim 1, wherein the dual-wavelength light sources comprise light sources operating at approximately 450 nm and 620 nm for illuminating the microplastic detection zone.
3.	The system of claim 1, wherein the primary polarizer and secondary cross polarizer are arranged substantially at 90° to suppress directly transmitted light and enhance detection of scattered light from suspended particles.
4.	The system of claim 1, wherein the photodiode receiver converts the detected scattered optical radiation into an electrical signal, and the signal-conditioning circuit amplifies, filters, and stabilizes the electrical signal.
5.	The system of claim 1, wherein the embedded microcontroller processes the conditioned electrical signal to determine the presence and approximate concentration of microplastics based on predefined detection criteria.
6.	The system of claim 1, further comprising a Wi-Fi communication module and cloud database configured to transmit, store, and remotely monitor microplastic measurement data.
7.	The system of claim 6, further comprising a web monitoring dashboard configured to display real-time and historical microplastic measurements.
8.	The system of claim 1, further comprising an automatic alert system configured to generate an alert when the detected microplastic concentration exceeds a predefined threshold.
9.	The system of claim 1, further comprising a rechargeable battery backup, voltage regulation circuit, local display, status indicators, data storage memory, control buttons, and a waterproof protective enclosure configured to support continuous field deployment of the system.
